title: ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Bring Raw Intensity to Tim Blake Nelson’s Death Row Drama
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 7:03am Amanda Seyfried in 'The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd.' Benoit Soler One of the principal takeaways from Tim Blake Nelson ’s bruising drama set in and around a maximum-security Oklahoma prison, The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd , is how infrequently we get to see Scoot McNairy in a meaty lead role that gives the reliably great character actor real complexity to chew on. McNairy plays a death row inmate who forms a connection with the equally compelling Amanda Seyfried ’s creative writing teacher, a woman stuck in an abusive marriage and grasping to find a way out. There’s ambiguity in both characters’ choices, making for a tough film that refuses to provide easy answers. Related Stories Movies 'Re/Pair' Review: David Schwimmer, W. Kamau Bell and Van Jones Lead Pragmatic Doc About the Past and Present of Black-Jewish Relations Movies THR Returns to TIFF With Editorial Portrait Studio, Video Lounge and Live 'Awards Chatter' Recording With Penélope Cruz Nelson took 12 years to get the project made, and that labor-of-love aspect shows in the soulfulness and meticulous care the writer-director brings to this unsettling story of violence begetting violence, based on actual events. He gathers what seems a hand-picked cast of excellent actors to breathe texture and authenticity into a drama that’s not an easy watch but should find an appreciative audience on streaming platforms. The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd The Bottom Line Grim but riveting. Venue : Toronto International Film Festival (Gala Presentations) Cast : Amanda Seyfried, Scoot McNairy, Missi Pyle, Devyn Tyler, Elizabeth Marvel, Tim Blake Nelson, Grant Harvey, William Jackson Harper, Wunmi Mosaku Director-screenwriter : Tim Blake Nelson 2 hours 1 minute Nelson doesn’t shy away from the horrific brutality at the heart of the film but nor does he sensationalize it in the interest of amping up the material into a crime thriller. The movie is notable for its thoughtful approach to themes more often explored via heightened emotions. Nelson’s measured handle on the drama gives it an imposing gravity. The seemingly counterintuitive backing of a delicate, predominantly acoustic guitar score by Henry Nelson and Will Curry places the film in the American heartland and signals from the start that the focus will be more psychological than action-driven. Seyfried plays Karen, recently returned to her hometown to be near her father, who has dementia and has been placed in an elder-care facility, which she has to pay for given that her brother is in prison. With high school teaching positions in short supply, she takes a spot teaching a group of a dozen or so inmates at a men’s prison, starting them off with a Hemingway story. Karen encourages the students to write something personal and is surprised to get back a beautifully shaped piece of prose from Wilson, recounting a childhood episode when he was hunting squirrels in the woods and the complicated way it made him feel about the act of killing. Nelson, who also appears as the prison warden, builds the film along three parallel timelines, detailing Karen’s prison classes, which become a strange kind of respite from her miserable time at home with Kenneth (Grant Harvey), her deadbeat drunk of a husband; Wilson’s escape with two other men and the shocking incident that adds a handful more deaths to the grisly murder conviction that put him away; and the ticking clock as senior state prison warden Joan Gardner ( Missi Pyle ) oversees preparations for the execution of an inmate by lethal injection, to be supervised by a specialized medic ( Elizabeth Marvel ). This ambitious tripartite structure comes with strengths and weaknesses. It gives the drama a disturbing sense of human beings’ capability for heartless violence, keeps us on edge and shakes up our perspective by intercutting sympathetic scenes with chilling ones. But it also makes for an initial challenge in figuring out where the three timelines sit in relation to each other. This is somewhat detrimental to the development of Karen, since cutting back and forth interrupts the flow of her epistolary relationship with Wilson, whose stories morph into intimate letters. Seyfried has no trouble putting across the desperation of a woman in an unendurable marriage, but the script rushes through the escalation of her exchanges with Wilson, making it harder to buy the degree to which she is willing to compromise herself by becoming an accomplice in his escape plan. Of course, the sad phenomenon of women falling under the spell of incarcerated men is well-documented, but some audiences might find themselves thinking Karen is too smart to be pulled in so deep. McNairy leans into the enigmatic side of Wilson. He has the voice of a richly expressive writer, implying sensitivity and humanity alongside his unquestionable intelligence, but also the coiled danger and volatility of an unrepentantly calculating killer. Did he court Karen’s complicity from the start or did the plan coalesce in stages once the unexplained bruises and cuts on her face pointed to violence at home, exposing her loneliness and vulnerability? Putting his lean and sinewy physicality to disquieting use, McNairy makes Wilson both unreadable and coldly transparent, giving him equal parts menace and magnetism. The most harrowing scenes follow an innocent family, John Lawson ( William Jackson Harper ), his wife Jane (Devyn Tyler) and their two sweet young kids. Jane’s belief in forgiveness crashes up against the far less categorical reality of a vicious world when the Lawsons are dropped into a situation of extreme terror. Harper and Tyler’s performances are heartstopping. There’s expert work also from Pyle as a careworn law enforcement officer unable to remain indifferent to the taking of another life in the the name of the law. A terrific scene in which Joan unburdens herself of troubling thoughts resonates throughout the execution, which Nelson makes the effective choice to show in unflinchingly clinical detail. Like other death row dramas including Clemency , Just Mercy and Dead Man Walking , this film questions whether there’s really that big a difference between murderous cruelty and state-sanctioned capital punishment. The one disappointment of the superb ensemble is that Sinners standout Wunmi Mosaku is given too little to do as a supportive friend to Karen, who takes her in when she’s forced to flee from Kenneth. But this is nonetheless a fascinatingly dark and uncompromising film that reaffirms Nelson’s standing as a vital force in American independent filmmaking for more than three decades. title: The Old & New Hollywood Guard Wielding AI’s Might
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 7:01am PT The Old & New Hollywood Guard Wielding AI’s Might A look at 10 companies that are looking to mold cutting-edge tech into must-have tools for the industry By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest James Cameron’s Lightstorm Scoops Up AI-Powered 3D Tech Company Outsyders 23 hours ago Universal Music Group Sues DistroKid for Deceptive Trade Practices and Building an ‘AI-Slop Pipeline’ 2 days ago Interview With Tilly Norwood Reveals Even Fewer Reasons For the Existence of the AI ‘Actress’ 3 days ago See All ILLUSTRATION: MICHAEL STARBUCK/VARIETY VIP+ The AI gold rush has hit showbiz, even as the tech-fueled race to riches remains fraught. Morphing at a mind-bendingly fast pace, artificial intelligence technology has roiled the entertainment industry, which remains split between those convinced that it can be a powerful tool for creative expression and those wary of i ts potential to introduce “cinema illiteracy” and cut humans out of the equation. Variety takes a look at how 10 companies are taming the AI beast with specific use cases that creatives can get behind in a way that keeps them firmly in control and respects copyrights. Related Stories Filmax Launches Mar Olid’s ‘The Wedding Hustlers’ (EXCLUSIVE) Markus Lehmusruusu’s Finnish Oscar Entry ‘The Squirrel’ Earns Aki Kaurismäki’s Stamp of Approval: ‘He Said It’s Like ‘2001: A Space Odyssey,’ but Better Because It’s Full of Humanism’ Some of the industry’s household names have been at the forefront of AI. This spring Netflix announced the surprise acquisition of Ben Affleck’s InterPositive AI start-up. Amazon MGM and Lionsgate have both appointed AI leaders, and Google, a foe and friend alike to creatives, has partnered with Oscar-winning talent through its DeepMind unit in a bid to strengthen its relationship with filmmakers. Popular on Variety Alongside the old guard, there’s a new one: a collection of companies not afraid to ruffle feathers, promising an unprecedented — and controversial — leap in how films are made. Such is the case with Particle 6 , the brash creator of AI “actress” Tilly Norwood, and the rabble-rousers at Higgsfield . Both upstarts have produced or are producing AI-generated films to showcase their technology. Other creative-minded AI companies include Runway , which is bullish on the democratization of filmmaking, and the Martin Scorsese-backed Black Forest Labs . What’s behind Hollywood’s new AI arms race? “It’s a maturing of some of the tools where it actually can be used now,” says Erik Weaver, the principal of AI and emergent media at the University of Southern California’s Entertainment Technology Center. And at the same time, “a lot of the studios are also seeing that land rush,” he adds — meaning, in other words, that they see the need to get on board or get left behind. Netflix last year said it was “all in” on incorporating AI throughout its business, but it was unclear exactly what that meant. Then it spent nearly $600 million on Ben Affleck’s secret AI company. The purchase of the tools-focused InterPositive in March signaled both the company’s investment in the space — with Affleck’s filmmaking background and film-focused team as the core drivers behind the purchase — and its belief in partnering with creatives as it experiments with the technology. Since then, Netflix has revealed that roughly 300 programs across its library have incorporated generative AI in some fashion, it’s experimenting with AI-animated projects (though none are actively in the works) and it has worked with the AI audio firm ElevenLabs to weave in an AI replica of Gene Wilder’s voice for its upcoming reality show “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket.” For some, the endorsement from the world’s biggest streamer helped validate AI’s presence in entertainment. “We really wanted to help folks contextualize and understand that AI is impacting all different parts of the production chain, and some of the examples from our different filmmakers using it kind of hit at the core of that kind of thesis,” says Girish Balakrishnan, Netflix’s senior director of creative innovation, about disclosing the 300 AI-enabled projects. “But kind of in [how] creator-led, filmmakers leading those productions are doing it, and we just want folks to be aware that that’s the state of things.” It’s an approach adopted by Amazon MGM, the tech giant’s studio arm that has developed its own AI wing. The studio last year appointed Albert Cheng, previously head of Prime Video in the U.S., as its inaugural head of “AI Studios” and charged him with integrating — though not mandating — the technology’s use throughout its production pipeline. Since then, Amazon MGM has hosted its “AI on the Lot” conference to discuss AI’s place in Hollywood, where it announced a slate of AI-animated shows (though one, from “The Book of Life” director Jorge R. Gutierrez, ended after Gutierrez backed out following an outcry over his plans for an AI-animated project). “AI helps the production pipeline move faster, so our customers won’t have to wait 24 months between seasons of a show,” Cheng says. “The goal is to figure out how we can put these tools into creators’ hands to help them make more series, more movies.” Not to be outdone, Lionsgate appointed industry veteran Kathleen Grace as its first-ever chief AI officer in February, tasking her with overseeing the studio’s strategy regarding the tech. The company hasn’t unveiled plans for how it’s using AI with its own IP, but in June expanded its yearslong deal with Runway through acquiring an equity stake to tap into one of its franchises for an AI-generated short-form series. “The thing we’re interested in is how do we use generative AI to find new opportunities and new audiences for the content we own?” Grace says. “New ways to distribute it, new ways to think about it, and that, to me, is the interesting thing about AI. It’s not just an efficiency play. It’s ‘Can we bring new life or new audiences to things by either using the intelligence that it offers us to make us distribute it more effectively or smartly?’ Or use AI and large language models and large amounts of social intelligence data to understand, ‘Oh, maybe there’s a subculture that is really into this movie that we have in our catalog, and we should be marketing it to them.’” Google, meanwhile, has tried to integrate itself into the creative community. The internet company has rankled some in entertainment and media over how it has trained its AI models. But Eli Collins, DeepMind’s vice president of product, says the company helps build custom models for many of its partnerships, such as the AI-powered production of “The Wizard of Oz” at the Sphere in Las Vegas, and will potentially be involved in the upcoming “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” at the venue. That’s helped earn the trust of directors like Darren Aronofsky, whose AI studio Primordial Soup partnered with Google, and director Doug Liman, who helped develop an immersive film, “Asteroid,” for the company’s extended-reality app. “When we work within a domain, we think it’s really critical to work with people in that domain,” Collins says. In video, “we’ve worked with people, industrial designers, we’ve worked with illustrators, and as videos progress, that’s really allowed us to go more into film and storytelling generally as a medium.” Google’s AI entertainment push included a $75 million investment this summer in indie film darling A24, which is researching new tools in partnership with DeepMind. That pact spawned a backlash among those incredulous that A24 was getting in the AI game; responding to the brouhaha, A24 said, “We’d rather have a seat at the table than [sit] on the sidelines.” Collins is tight-lipped about that partnership, as well as the company’s potential involvement in the Sphere’s upcoming production of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” As established studios and big tech companies plant their AI flags, a new crop of disruptors has emerged. Particle 6, the U.K. company behind Tilly Norwood, caused a firestorm over the boisterous claim the “actor” would soon be signed to an agency (agencies said “no thanks” ) and stirred fears that Tilly would take actors’ jobs (leading to new SAG-AFTRA guidelines on synthetic performers). CEO Eline Van der Velden says the industry got it wrong. She says Tilly’s whole purpose is to exist for “underserved” audiences and that the AI character was never intended to replace human actors. “Everything would need to be AI,” she said. “That’s where Tilly makes sense.” Van der Velden says the controversial Tilly-led film “Misaligned,” which kicked off an anticipated 12-month production cycle this month, is simply meant for those audiences eager for more “niche” content. She also thinks Tilly herself could be a new model for human actors to work with, akin to motion capture. “In a way, I’m a puppeteer, because especially when I’m doing motion capture, where I’m the creative director of her acting,” she says. “This is what I think actors in the future will be in charge of.” For companies invested in the intersection of AI and entertainment, much of the work to date has been proofs-of-concept. Fountain 0 ’s debut of the docudrama “Dreams of Violets” at the Tribeca Festival in June made it one of the first fully AI-generated films to premiere at a major festival. The company also made a knockoff of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” dubbed “Odysseus: The Fall,” hoping to show how close the technology can get to producing a similar version of a $250 million summer blockbuster. (Unsurprisingly, not everyone agreed that it was in the same ballpark.) Ash Koosha, CEO of Fountain 0, says his goal is to help people execute their own visions for movies, without the dozens of crew members typically needed for a feature film. The company also inked a deal with “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin, who licensed her likeness to the company to help adapt her novels. “I think we’re going to see with AI the power of a $400 million film, the look of it, the reality of it, in the hand of an arthouse filmmaker,” he says. Along those lines, Runway and Higgsfield have made moves to get their respective generative-AI platforms into the hands of aspiring filmmakers. Higgsfield has hosted contests and inked likeness- licensing partnerships , while Runway has held its AI Festival each year since 2022. Both companies have given creators a chance to bring their stories and intellectual property to life, a la the director Kane Parsons’ journey from YouTube creator to theaters with his thriller “Backrooms.” “New technology unlocks new creative formats, and this is just another example of the sort of IP or celebrities crossover, something which they couldn’t do typically,” Higgsfield CEO Alex Mashrabov says. “This is just a great example of how a traditional story, how a traditional script, can be applied to these modern realities.” Runway’s festivals have drawn the likes of director Ron Howard and Netflix’s Balakrishnan. Co-CEO Cristóbal Valenzuela says the company plans to drop “AI” from the title next year in the spirit of its belief that, after this moment of “transition,” the use of AI will be as commonplace in cinema as cameras. A future like that takes the backing of those who know how to make movies — and some heavyweights have come out in support of using AI tools in the craft. “I don’t think there’s going to be a day or a time or a month when someone’s gonna say, ‘OK, this is the day we stop saying this is AI video or not AI video,’” Valenzuela says. “It just happens naturally. It’s a transition, and we’re going through a transition right now.” Scorsese’s backing of the German AI company Black Forest Labs represented the most public endorsement from a film visionary of the technology’s place in the production process. But for the company itself, it was a partnership tied to research and exploration of how the tools could work for creatives. While Scorsese hasn’t commented on the partnership (and the start-up won’t say whether he’s using its Flux models on his next film), the revelation of his participation marked another divisive moment for the industry. “AI in the creative space is an emotive issue,” says Ben Brooks, Black Forest’s head of public policy. “We’re sensitive to the depth of feeling across the community, but at the same time, building these bridges, having this kind of dialogue, is really important to understand how we can make the technology work for the community.” How fully Hollywood deploys AI may be held in check by one key factor: Public sentiment appears to remain strongly against the technology’s use in movies and TV. Social media users flamed the use of AI in Eli Roth’s “Ice Cream Man” and the David Dastmalchian-led “Late Night With the Devil,” among others. Many people fear AI’s societal impact. Director Jon Erwin, who founded Innovative Dreams , an AI offshoot of his Amazon-affiliated Wonder Project initiative that fuses generative technology into its projects, thinks such fears stem from people lumping productive use cases together with forms of AI “slop.” Erwin, who has incorporated generative-AI technology into his Amazon MGM show “House of David” and his Angel Studios film “Young Washington,” says artificial intelligence should be seen as part of the long arc of technology adoption by creators. “There is a collision of technology and art,” Erwin says. “Hollywood has always been an art form that is a fusion of tools that are disruptive and given to artists — and used in ways no one would expect.” *** Amazon MGM Studios AI focus : Company in May greenlit three shows under its “GenAI Creators’ Fund,” including shows from “Book of Life” director Jorge Gutierrez (who backed out) and ex-Nickelodeon president Albie Hecht; the home of Jon Erwin’s shows, adopting the filmmaker’s use of the technology; developed “Project Nara” with AWS, a workspace for creators using AI. Key player : Albert Cheng, head of AI studios Why they matter: The studio arm of the e-commerce behemoth is in pole position among major studios to harness the power of proprietary tech, prodigious computing power and top-tier content production. Black Forest Labs Image and video generator AI focus : Martin Scorsese put the company on the map when he cited it as helping him plot out the storyboard for an upcoming film. Investors include BroadLight Capital and CAA co-founder Mike Ovitz. Key players : David Dorfman, co-founder and managing partner; Kevin Yorn and Rick Yorn, co-founders and general partners Why they matter: Because Martin Scorsese said so. Fountain 0 Filmmaking and streaming platform AI focus : “Dreams of Violets” accepted into Tribeca, a breakthrough for AI movies; recently licensed “The View” host Sunny Hostin’s image for AI movie adaptations of her romance novels. Key player: Ash Koosha, creator and CEO Why they matter: Koosha has an expansive vision of what AI filmmaking can achieve. Google DeepMind AI research laboratory AI focus : Its work with filmmakers Doug Liman and Darren Aronofsky and A24 underscore its pursuit of Hollywood. It’s also focused on AI experiences, like “The Wizard of Oz” at the Sphere in Las Vegas, and its potential involvement in the venue’s “Rocky Horror Picture Show” production. Key player : Eli Collins, VP of product for Google DeepMind, Márcia Mayer, head of production for DeepMind Why they matter: Because they’re part of Google. Higgsfield AI AI video platform AI focus : “Hell Grind” and “Cully Hill Boys” showcased what an AI-generated action-adventure could look like — even if the final product wasn’t great; AI-assisted films and licensing influencers’ likenesses for a project. Key player : Alex Mashrabov, CEO and founder Why they matter: Higgsfield has hosted AI contests and inked likeness-licensing pacts. Innovative Dreams Virtual production studio AI focus : Director Jon Erwin has forged an indie path through his Wonder Project venture, and he’s also been a maverick who has publicly embraced the efficiency of AI tools to enable creatives. The filmmaker’s production technology venture Innovative Dreams launched earlier this year with AI firm Luma. Key players : Jon Erwin, Luma CEO Amit Jain Why they matter: Wonder Project has impressed by building an indie film and TV business in just a few years since its 2021 launch. AI’s potential could turbocharge that growth and Erwin’s experimentation could attract others to his firm’s tech. Lionsgate AI focus : In 2024, the studio set a deal to train an AI model on the company’s film library in order to generate new content. It also hired its first-ever AI division head. Key player : Kathleen Grace, chief AI officer Why they matter: Lionsgate has the kind of huge library that could be attractive to a content-hungry AI firm with deep pockets. The studio is seen as a bellwether for Hollywood M&A. Netflix AI focus : The streaming giant says flatly that more than 300 of its programs use AI in production. It surprised the industry with a $587 million deal to buy Ben Affleck’s InterPositive startup. It’s even bankrolling Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s AI thriller “2034.” Key players: Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters; Girish Balakrishnan, senior director of creative innovation; Ben Affleck Why they matter: Because they’re Netflix. Particle 6 Content studio AI focus : The company is home to the synthetic actress Tilly Norwood, whose debut as a film festival PR stunt triggered fears about AI creations taking the place of human actors. Key players : CEO Eline Van der Velden Why they matter : Love Tilly or hate Tilly, Van der Velden has proven her ability to garner attention and spur outrage among anti-AI purists. Runway AI research, audio and video image generation AI focus : A leader in AI generation and exhibition; expansive partnership with Lionsgate to work on IP illustrates how Hollywood is willing to cede its most valuable assets to AI models; showcases AI films at its annual bi-coastal festival, which this year saw its biggest turnout and included Ron Howard. Key player : Cristóbal Valenzuela, co-founder and CEO Why they matter: The former NYU Tisch researcher has gained the trust of major filmmakers and studios to help them learn how to use AI tools. title: ‘Elf’ Movie to Come to Life With Immersive Experience at NYC’s Rockefeller Center (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All September 17, 2026 7:00am Will Ferrell in 'Elf.' New Line/courtesy Everett Collection Elf fans will have a unique way to spread Christmas cheer during this holiday season. The world of New Line Cinema’s beloved film Elf is set to come alive at HERO in New York City ‘s Rockefeller Center with The Elf Experience . The all-new immersive holiday adventure begins Nov. 14 from Warner Bros. Global Experiences and Fairview Portals. HERO, which is Rockefeller Center’s venue devoted to immersive storytelling, will transform into a storybook journey at the North Pole in honor of director Jon Favreau ‘s enduring 2003 movie that starred Will Ferrell as Buddy, a man raised by elves. The experience will involve immersive environments, interactive activities, photo opportunities and special treats, all inspired by the film itself. Related Stories Business Paramount Argues That the States Post a $1.88 Billion Bond to Cover Warner Bros. Bills TV 'New York: A Documentary Film' Returns to PBS With Two New Episodes on the 21st Century (Exclusive) Guests to The Elf Experience will meet one of Santa’s helpers before entering Papa Elf’s storybook and heading to the North Pole to learn about the life of an elf. The journey will include stops at the Candy Cane Forest, the Sea of Swirly Twirly Gumdrops, Santa’s Toy Workshop, the North Pole and ultimately New York City and Gimbels. The Elf Experience will offer a range of merchandise, such as apparel, accessories, toys, treats and artist collaborations. “We’ve assembled a group of artists that worked on the original film, as well as new ones who were inspired by it,” says Favreau, filmmaker and founder of Fairview Portals. “Miniature work, forced perspective, zoetrope and animatronics were all implemented to create a unique and handcrafted experience to capture the spirit of the film.” Elf Tickets are now available online for The Elf Experience , with prices starting at $45 for adults and $35 for children. It opens to the public on Saturday, Nov. 14. Adds Warner Bros. Discovery president of global experiences and worldwide studio operations Simon Robinson, “Watching Elf has become a holiday tradition for millions of fans, and Rockefeller Center is synonymous with the holidays in New York City. Bringing the two together gives fans from New York and around the world an entirely new way to immerse themselves in the Elf story. Together with Fairview Portals, it is a privilege to bring the humor, heart and Christmas cheer of Elf to life in this state-of-the-art experience . “ THR

title: MLW Finally Gets Its Tubi Deal (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 17, 2026 7:00am Major League Wrestling's flagship series 'MLW Fusion' is headed to Tubi. MLW At long last, MLW ( Major League Wrestling ) is headed to Tubi under a new deal. Starting tonight, Thursday, Sept. 17 at 8 p.m. ET, the pro-wrestling promotion’s flagship series MLW Fusion will stream (for free) live on the on-demand/FAST platform. News episodes will premiere each Thursday in the same time slot. This was actually the deal that was meant to happen five years ago. At the time, however, WWE allegedly pressured Tubi into canceling the deal, leveraging its relationship with Tubi-owner Fox — WWE’s SmackDown aired on the broadcast network back then. The done deal was undone the night before I was set to exclusively report it. WWE and MLW settled out of court, with the former paying the latter $20 million. Related Stories Movies 'Resident Evil' Review: Zach Cregger Gives a Fatigued Franchise an Exhilarating Shot in the Arm Movies Zach Cregger's 'Resident Evil': First Reactions From the Premiere MLW has undergone some significant changes since then. For starters, actor Paul Walter Hauser has joined Court Bauer and Bryan Walsh as executive producer; additionally, Major League Wrestling signed with Artists First for representation in March 2025. And in fall 2025, MLW partnered with Danny McBride’s Don Gato Tequila and moved its headquarters from New York to Charleston, South Carolina. Tubi has 110 million monthly active users. MLW Fusion was relaunched in May 2026; the company’s pay-per-view events are now distributed by Live Nation’s Veeps. MLW Fusion episodes are also available on Veeps and NJPW World. “Wrestling should be easy to find and free to watch,” said Bauer, the founder and CEO of Major League Wrestling. “We built MLW around that, no paywalls, no subscription barriers, nothing standing between a fan and the show, and Tubi shares that same fan-first philosophy at scale. Starting Sept. 17, Tubi’s 110 million monthly active users have a front row seat on Thursday nights to the hardest hitting hour in pro wrestling, and it won’t cost a dime.” MLW Fusion “serves up a distinctive brand of pro wrestling, blending cutting-edge, new-era wrestling with the grit, colorful characters and throwback flavor of ’rasslin,” the company says. “Built around big fights, heated rivalries, championship stakes and an anything-can-happen attitude, Fusion brings a rowdy, hard-hitting edge to the modern wrestling landscape. MLW will also continue to produce live special events alongside the weekly series.” THR

title: ‘This Week’ Executive Producer Ready to Scramble for Midterms
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 7:00am PT ‘This Week’ Executive Producer Ready to Scramble for Midterms By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest CookUnity Serves Gourmet Meals in New York City Bodegas With Spicy Promotional Recipe 41 minutes ago CNBC Bolsters Staff Devoted to DTC, Streaming 1 day ago ‘60 Minutes’ Season Debut Sees 21% Drop in Ratings: Is NFL or CBS News to Blame? 2 days ago See All ABC Few people have their lives scrambled at 2 a.m. on a Sunday morning, but for Jon Schlossberg , such stuff can be quite routine. Not too long ago, Schlossberg, still only a few months into his tenure as the new executive producer of the ABC News Sunday public-affairs program “This Week,” found out in the wee hours of a Sunday morning that Senator Lindsay Graham has passed away. Suddenly, the lineup of the show he oversees needed to be redone – and quickly. Related Stories Peter Jackson's Weta FX to Talk AI as Netflix's Creative Asia Spotlights 'Possible Love' in Busan ‘The Nature of Invisible Things’ Director Rafaela Camelo Lines Up Luciana Paes and Sundance-Winner Camila Márdila For ‘The Favorite Daughter’ (EXCLUSIVE) “It’s our job on ‘This Week” to follow the news. That can lead to some very exciting last-minute decisions,” confesses Schlossberg, who took the reins of the program. “We enter the weekend with a plan and wake up early Sunday and see where we are.” Popular on Variety As “This Week” finishes the 2025-2026 season, the program kept its status as the nation’s most-watched Sunday public-affairs show for the fifth consecutive cycle, according to data from Nielsen. “This Week” commanded an average of 2.726 million viewers for the cycle, compared with 2.634 million for CBS’ “Face the Nation” and 2.588 million for NBC’s “Meet the Press.” The NBC program leads among viewers between 25 and 54, the age demographic most coveted by advertisers in news programming. Schlossberg is increasingly focused on the run-up to the midterm elections in November. He believes the rotation of three moderators at “This Week” — George Stephanopoulos, Jonathan Karl and Martha Raddatz — lends the program a distinction against rivals. Stephanopoulos is “keenly interested in impactful investigative work,” says Schlossbrerg, looking at “money in politics, and how it affects power in Washington and doing big interviews.” Karl “loves to do big interviews on the road,” talking to people across the nation about their view on data centers. title: Cary Joji Fukunaga, Sine Plambech Named Zurich Film Festival’s Feature and Documentary Jury Presidents
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 6:40am Cary Joji Fukunaga, Sine Plambech Zurich Film Festival has confirmed its feature film competition jury will be presided over by James Bond director Cary Joji Fukunaga , while filmmaker Sine Plambech will head up the documentary competition jury. American director and screenwriter Fukunaga ( No Time to Die ) will be joined on his jury by Swiss-French actress Ella Rumpf ( Love Letters ), Mexican director and screenwriter Fernando Eimbcke ( Moscas ), producer Julie Billy ( The Little Sister ), and Italian film editor and director Walter Fasano ( Nino – Un Film Su Nino Rota ). They will decide on the winner of the Golden Eye in the feature film competition. Related Stories News King Charles Makes Rare Statement Over Bombshell Memoir Claim He Told Diana's Brother: "We'll Forget Her Soon Enough" Movies Zhang Yimou to Lead Busan Film Festival Competition Jury Among the 14 movies vying for the Golden Eye is Rhys Marc Jones’ Black Church Bay , a mystery-thriller starring Tom Cullen and Joe Locke about a man whose world unravels after an intimate encounter with a younger man. Zou Jing’s A Girl Unknown , Blerta Basholli’s Dua and Pierre le Gall’s Flesh and Fuel are also included in the competition section, as are Andrina Mračnikar’s Mila / Marija , Manuela Martelli’s El Deshielo , Ramzi Bashour’s Hot Water , Fabian Stumm’s Die Ideen , Tareq Daoud’s Serife Tavsan , Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri’s Clarissa , Mads Mengel Nielsen’s The Guest , Ghasideh Golmakani’s Head to Head , Andrius Blaževičius’s How to Divorce During the War and Ufuk Emiroglu’s Sevda . Meanwhile, Danish anthropologist and filmmaker Sine Plambech ( Heartbound ) will head up the doc competition jury with Spanish cinematographer Alfredo de Juan ( Edge of the Unknown ), Norwegian producer Anne Köhncke ( Pervert Park ), Swiss director Jela Hasler ( Les Nouvelles Eves ) and Austrian director and producer Nikolaus Geyrhalter ( Homo Sapiens ). Fourteen films are competing in the doc section, including Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco’s Cannes-premiering The Match , following the historic Argentina vs. England game at the 1986 FIFA World Cup, as well as Habiba Nosheen’s The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony and Guillaume Massart’s Le Detention . Christian Bonke and Adam Bonke will present Perfect Road , chronicling a man living as a nomad on his bicycle for 10 years, and Elisabeth Rasmussen’s We Are Stardust , Erik Shirai’s Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing , Gar O’Rourke’s The Siege of Paradise , Simon David’s Shreckschraube and Lucas Paleocrassas’ Bugboy . Pete Muller will compete with Bucks Harbor , as will Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ One In a Million , Khoroldorj Choijoovanchig’s Colors of White Rock , Patrick Wally’s My Home of Wind and Sand and Arnaud Alain’s La Face Cachee De La Terre . BUCKS HARBOR (Pete Muller, USA, 2026) Highlights from this year’s Zurich Film Festival gala lineup include Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky , Beth de Araújo’s Josephine starring Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan, Possible Love , the new drama from acclaimed Korean director Lee Chang-dong ( Burning ), and Wicker , the sci-fi fantasy rom-com from directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson starring Alexander Skarsgård, Olivia Colman, and Elizabeth Debicki. Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid and Bunker with Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz will also screen. Julianne Moore is set to be honored with the Golden Icon Award and will accept the accolade alongside Jesse Eisenberg, who directs her in his latest feature The Debut , a musical-comedy co-starring Paul Giamatti. John Turturro will be honored with the Golden Eye Award. He’s being recognized for his performance in Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , a project that is already garnering awards buzz . The 22nd Zurich Film Festival takes place from Sept. 24-Oct. 4. THR

title: CookUnity Serves Gourmet Meals in New York City Bodegas With Spicy Promotional Recipe
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 6:20am PT CookUnity Serves Gourmet Meals in New York City Bodegas With Spicy Promotional Recipe By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest CookUnity Serves Gourmet Meals in New York City Bodegas With Spicy Promotional Recipe 32 minutes ago CNBC Bolsters Staff Devoted to DTC, Streaming 24 hours ago ‘60 Minutes’ Season Debut Sees 21% Drop in Ratings: Is NFL or CBS News to Blame? 2 days ago See All Courtesy of CookUnity How do you get consumers to pick one subscription food-delivery service over another? Perhaps by serving up something a little different on the marketing front. CookUnity launched in 2016, with the premise of tweaking the recipe in the increasingly crowded business of serving meals to harried consumers who have little time to cook or prepare dinner. The independent company offers meals designed by top chefs such as Esther Choi, Jose Garces, and Marcus Samuelsson. Related Stories Zack Snyder Wants You to Know He’s No Fascist: ‘I Made the Gayest Movie Ever Made’ Its latest promotional effort aims to burnish its offerings to every New Yorker. On Thursday eight chefs set up shop – literally – at five local bodegas, delis or corner stores, serving up signature dishes for free to anyone who might walk in. John DeLucie, for example, grilled up rack of lamb, while Andrew Rea, also known as Babish, offered spicy chili-garlic noodles and Guinness shepherd’s pie. Popular on Variety “There are a lot of other providers of meals and subscription programs throughout the country,” acknowledges Michael Baruch, CookUnity’s head of brand. But the company believes it has a notable distinction that puts high quality dishes from celebrated chiefs in the hands of people who might ordinarily might not be able to sample them. “We don’t make any food. What we do is partner with the best chefs in the world,” he says, who take part because CookUnity’s distribution allows them to forge connections with customers not in the immediate vicinity of their restaurants. “Bodegas and delis and corner stores are part fo the cultural fabric of New York,” Baruch adds. Putting the chefs in these well-visited locations “provides access to individuals and communication with the chefs at a level people wouldn’t ordinarily have access to.” The global food subscription market size was valued at $6.19 billion in 2025, according to Fortune Business Insights, and is projected to grow to $14.4 billion in 2032, up from $6.74 billion in 2026. North American consumers create the biggest demand for such services. Chefs will also be handing out complete meals under seal that people can take home and eat later and offer “little bites” at the bodegas that can be sampled. Guests can also scratch a bodega-style lottery ticket for a chance to win free CookUnity meals for a year and additional prizes including special dining experiences at participating chefs’ restaurants. The promotion will, hopefully “give bodega owners a day off,” says Baruch, and “create some energy in these stores” that will get consumers to sample new foods and forge different connections with chefs. They will also promote appearances, he says, on their own social channels. Jessica Chastain to Star in New Netflix Drama Series ‘The Retrievals’ Loading comments... title: José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown”
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown” ‘Onwards And Sideways’ Team Rhys Ifans, Laura Linney & John Madden On Making A Parkinson’s Story That Finds Laughter & Love In The Unexpected — Toronto Former DreamWorks & MGM TV Exec Brian Edwards Teams With Alpha Film Founders To Launch Time Zone Capital View All September 17, 2026 6:13am José Luis Rebordinos San Sebastian International Film Festival As the San Sebastián International Film Festival kicks into gear this weekend, it will be a bittersweet moment for José Luis Rebordinos. The longtime festival director is stepping down after what will be his 17th edition this year with deputy director Maialen Beloki taking over in January 2027. “Maialen is a highly qualified professional with an in-depth knowledge of the festival,” Rebordinos tells Deadline. “She has been part of the team for seventeen years, serving as deputy director for the last eleven of those. I can’t think of anyone better suited to the role.” Related Stories News 'Club Kid' & 'The Man I Love' Among Titles Added To San Sebastian Lineup News Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' & Fred Cavayé's 'Les Misérables' Among Six New Titles In San Sebastián Official Selection While assured the festival is in good hands for its next chapter, Rebordinos says there are three things of which is he is most proud: “First there is the growth we have created in the industry activities, the second is that we have made it into a festival that works all year round with our school of cinema and residential projects and the third is the archive.” Watch on Deadline Indeed, San Sebastián has increasingly ramped up its industry activity during Rebordinos’ tenure and the Spanish event is now considered the premiere hub for connecting Europe’s film industry to Latin American cinema and filmmaking talents. In the past, the festival had supported early works of filmmakers such as Brazil’s Walter Salles to Argentina’s Daniel Burman whose respective early works Foreign Land and A Chrysanthemum Bursts in Cincoesquinas both screened at the festival. Rebordinos has built on that with sections such as its Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum, which started in 2012, and its Works in Progress LatAm, which was launched in 2020. In 2015, the festival started its Ikusmira Berriak residency program in partnership with the Tabakalera International Center for Contemporary Culture and Elías Querejeta Zine Eskola (EQZE). Filmmakers to emerge from that ecosystem include Chilean filmmaker Diego Céspedes with his feature The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo ( La misteriosa mirada del flamenco ), and Gabriel Azorín with his feature Last Night I Conquered the City of Tebas ( Anoche conquisté Tebas ). Céspedes’ project premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2025 where it took a top prize in Un Certain Regard while Azorín’s film premiered at Venice the same year. Since 2018, San Sebastián has also worked closely with EQZE on Artxiboa, a historical digital and physical archive of the festival that is dedicated to preserving and sharing seven decades of the festival’s history. It contains more than 15,000 paper documents, 17,000 photographs, press dossiers, journals and festival posters dating from the festival’s founding in 1953 to the present. San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference Deadline In 2022, San Sebastián teamed up with CAA Media Finance to launch an annual Creative Investors’ Conference, which runs during the festival and has seen the attendance of major international players such as CAA’s Roeg Sutherland, Goodfellas founder Vincent Maraval, Neon’s Tom Quinn and Mediawan’s Elisabeth d’Arvieu, “We have more and more people attending each year and it’s become incredibly successful,” says Rebordinos. “Business agreements have taken place here and it’s important that we have a relaxed atmosphere to support this. We are a smaller festival for a reason. We don’t want to be a very big festival. We want to be a human festival for industry activities. We are not a market – it’s impossible for us. We are a little city and a little festival but sometimes it’s good to be smaller.” Maraval, a longtime supporter of San Sebastián, notes that Rebordinos helped propel the festival “to another dimension.” “His sense of hospitality and his taste positioned San Sebastián in the top three international festivals,” says Maraval. “He knew how to take advantage of all of the assets of this beautiful city and make the festival unique.” He continues: “I won’t miss him because he became a friend and my friendship won’t stop because he is no longer in charge. We will continue our cinema discussion around a great meal, and I hope I will still benefit from his advice like when he told me to look at Los Javis’ work. His job is perhaps over but his taste remains.” Sutherland agrees noting that Rebordinos “has turned the festival into an international destination.” “Like Venice, San Sebastián is a launching pad for awards pictures, as well as a celebration of Spanish cinema and putting it at the forefront of our minds,” says the CAA exec. “In the last several years, he established a conference that brings together like-minded voices to address the needs of our industry and find solutions for the future and preservation of cinema.” Spanish producer Marisa Fernández Armenteros, whose film Sundays won the Golden Shell for Best Film at the festival last year, says: “Rebordinos is, above all, a hopeless optimist. I still remember the 2020 edition during the pandemic. Everything was being canceled and Rebordinos would call us to say, ‘Between optimism and pessimism, it is better for me to be an optimist. We’ll make it happen. There will be a festival.’ And he did. “I will always be grateful to him for calling me, whether it was to share good news or bad. He has always faced up to things, understanding that it is part of his responsibility. And the longer I work in this industry, the more I value that attitude. I have seen him quietly support directors and producers with their first films, as well as projects from Latin America that were stuck in financing limbo. And always, quietly, behind the scenes.” Rebordinos says he’s not leaving the industry completely and plans to consult with other festivals down the line on “matters relating to Spanish and Latin American cinema.” “But I won’t be on the front line,” he says. “Rather, I will always be working in support of others.” The 74 th San Sebastián International Film Festival takes place September 18-26, 2026. Zac Ntim contributed to this report. According to Nex, the company plans to roll out “connected play,” which will allow families to play together on its fitness-centric gaming consoles across households and distances. Led by CEO David Lee, Nex also plans to expand across Europe and Asia, following its recent expansion into Canada, the U.K. and the Republic of Ireland. Nex will move into Germany later this year, with Japan and Korea planned for 2027. Popular on Variety Related Stories Zack Snyder Wants You to Know He’s No Fascist: ‘I Made the Gayest Movie Ever Made’ Nex Playground ‘s current lineup consists of 60 games, including globally recognized franchises and characters such as “Bluey,” Barbie, “Kung Fu Panda” and “Peppa Pig,” with experiences spanning music, sports, fitness, party and learning. The slate will continue to grow this fall and holiday season with “NFL Flag,” “Dude Perfect Trickshot Challenge,” “PAC-MAN” with Bandai Namco Entertainment and more. The late-stage funding comes in the same year that Nex Playground crossed more than one million units sold, with the system now distributed across more than 7,000 U.S. retail locations, including Costco, Sam’s Club, Target, Walmart and Best Buy. Nex’s subscriber base has grown sevenfold over the past 18 months and is approaching 1 million subscribers, a milestone the company expects to surpass by year-end. This new round of financing includes a Series E led by Baillie Gifford and BAI Capital, with participation from NBA Investments, Logitech, Medici Capital Partners, and the Raine Group, alongside a new credit facility with JPMorgan. Additionally, Nex has brought on Niantic vet Jeff Shouger as its chief financial officer and set Shouger and gaming and technology industry veteran Bing Gordon as new members of the company’s board of directors. “Families have timeless needs: to move, grow, connect, and have fun. The response to Nex Playground has shown us that active play can serve those needs at a meaningful scale,” Lee said. “We are building Nex to be a 100-year company. This investment gives us the resources to bring active play to millions more families around the world, and Jeff and Bing bring extraordinary experience building enduring gaming and technology companies. I’m thrilled to have them with us for this next chapter.” Jessica Chastain to Star in New Netflix Drama Series ‘The Retrievals’ Loading comments... title: Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM Former Sony, Endemol & Talpa Exec Ziad Kebbi Takes The Reins At MForMedia As Dubai-Based Production Company Refocuses On Originals & AI View All September 17, 2026 6:00am Dhar Mann & Sean Atkins are headed to MIPCOM Cannes Ian Spanier, Justine Knight EXCLUSIVE: Dhar Mann is headed to Cannes for MIPCOM . The powerhouse digital producer will take a headline slot alongside Sean Atkins, CEO of Dhar Mann Studios . The pair will speak on Sunday, October 11, the day before the MIPCOM market opens. It marks the first time MIPCOM organizers have scheduled a pre-opening keynote in this way. The reality of the market is most folks arrive on the Sunday to be in position for proceedings, which start the next day. MIPCOM organizers said Mann and Atkins will break down how an audience-first creator business works. They will also cover how to build IP around communities, work up positive stories, and create new partnerships that link creators, brands and the entertainment business. Related Stories News Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM News 'Killing Eve' Origin Story 'Honey' To World Premiere At MIPCOM Mann majors in uplifting content aimed at a wide audience. DMS has 170M followers and its content registers 300M views every week. It operates out of a 125,000 sq. ft. studio in Burbank. Watch on Deadline It recently partnered with Disney with a deal for original programming and has inked a distribution deal with Fox Entertainment for a slate of vertical video titles. It has also partnered with brands including Adobe, the NFL, Microsoft and Gap. “Creators are building audiences at a scale that used to be possible only through traditional media, but what’s most exciting is when we turn that connection into franchises, new formats and partnerships that can travel around the world,” Mann said. “Sean and I are looking forward to coming to Cannes and sharing what we’ve learned scaling Dhar Mann Studios, and why we believe the future of entertainment will be shaped by creators and the traditional industry working much more closely together.” The MIPCOM activity comes as the event’s organizers, RX France, position it as more than a place to buy and sell TV shows. Under the stewardship of event director, Lucy Smith, it has pushed heavily into digital, branded content and the creator economy in recent editions. “Dhar Mann Studios is a powerful example of how creator-led businesses are reshaping the global entertainment industry,” Smith said. “Bringing Dhar and Sean to our main stage reflects MIPCOM’s role in bringing together the established entertainment business with the creators, platforms and new models shaping its future.” We hear DMS and MIPCOM will also co-host an invite-only dinner on the Sunday evening, bringing together about 25 CMOs and industry leaders for a pre-market get-together. MIPCOM runs from October 11-15. title: San Sebastián Film Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos On This Year’s Line-Up & Why Festivals “Have To Speak About Human Rights”
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown” ‘Onwards And Sideways’ Team Rhys Ifans, Laura Linney & John Madden On Making A Parkinson’s Story That Finds Laughter & Love In The Unexpected — Toronto Former DreamWorks & MGM TV Exec Brian Edwards Teams With Alpha Film Founders To Launch Time Zone Capital View All September 17, 2026 5:52am San Sebastian International Film Festival San Sebastian International Film Festival With the fall festival season underway, the international film community is now turning its head to Spain’s Basque Coast as the San Sebastian International Film Festival kicks off its 74th edition on September 18. With 263 projects from 47 countries in the official lineup, the program looks set to bring together a mix of established auteurs, emerging filmmakers and star power that continues to make it one of the most interesting European launchpads on the festival calendar. Tomorrow will see the event open with the world premiere of Fatih Akin’s fantasy drama Ghost Song , which will compete for the festival’s Golden Shell award. Further titles in the competition line up include Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut with Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti; Pablo Larraín’s Netflix horror series My Sad Dead ( Mis muertos tristes ); the world premiere of Fred Cavayé’s action-skewed adaptation of Les Misérables ; Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care ; Ah Biao’s Chinese-language feature debut Border ; and Nicole Garcia’s Marion Cotillard starrer Milo . The festival will close with Le Faux Soir from Belgian filmmaker Michaël R. Roskam on September 26. Related Stories News 'Club Kid' & 'The Man I Love' Among Titles Added To San Sebastian Lineup News Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' & Fred Cavayé's 'Les Misérables' Among Six New Titles In San Sebastián Official Selection “We are always very eclectic,” says San Sebastián Film Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos about the selection for his final edition at the festival. The well-respected veteran has been running the event since 2011 and is stepping down at the end of the year. Watch on Deadline “This year, we have a mix of commercial and more radical cinema,” he says. “I’m really happy that we have Les Misérables in competition because, for me, it’s a good example of popular French cinema. It’s a very good film and a big production that will be really popular with our audiences. At the same time, we have Border , a very radical, but very difficult and interesting film as well as Pablo Larraín’s My Sad Dead ( Mis muertos tristes ).” This year’s event will also pack star power, with Naomi Watts, Brad Pitt, Penelope Cruz, Cotillard, Orlando Bloom, Rami Malek and Diego Luna among expected attendees. Watts will be the recipient of the festival’s prestigious Donostia Award, and she’ll touch down to screen her latest film The Housewife , the directorial debut of Canadian helmer Ben Shirinian. Director Werner Herzog will also receive a Donostia Award this year, while Pitt and director David Ayer will screen their latest film Heart of the Beast , which is set to play out of competition. It will mark Pitt’s first trip to the festival since 2009, when he and Quentin Tarantino presented Inglourious Basterds there. Ira Sachs will preside over the competition jury this year. “One of the most important sections for the festival is the New Directors section because we are very free and open when we select them,” says Rebordinos. “This year, I think the new directors we have selected in the section are more courageous than ever.” The New Directors strand includes first or second-time directors from Bulgaria, Chile, Germany, Iran, Japan, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Norway, South Korea, Spain, Taiwan, the UK and Ukraine. It will open with The Bad Son ( El mal hijo ), the debut feature from Jaime Lorente. The film’s official synopsis reads: When 11-year-old Ruben’s father mysteriously disappears, the boy has to move in with his grandmother, a woman he barely knows. In a rural setting, where time seems to have stood still, the child will learn that family wounds are passed down from one generation to another and will try to find a way to heal them as he grows. Les Miserables Curiosa Films – Eskwad – Studiocanal – TF1 Films production – Photo by Christophe Brachet “I think it’s a good moment for the new directors,” continues Rebordinos, pointing to Jordan Firstman’s feature debut Club Kid , which premiered in Cannes and saw A24 acquire the title for $17M in a competitive situation. Firstman rose to fame during the pandemic through is viral satirical impression videos on Instagram. Club Kid will screen in San Sebastián’s Perlak strand, which comprises a selection of feature films that have yet to be released in Spain but have had critical acclaim at other international festivals. Further titles in that lineup include Pawel Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord , Na Hong-jin’s Hope , Olivia Wilde’s The Invite and Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine . “The lineup really reflects the situation of cinema at this moment, in that it is very complex and different,” Rebordinos says. “Our official selection is definitely one of the most interesting lineups we have had in years. Cinema tends to reflect the society from which it originates and that’s why this year some titles reflect the way people film for Instagram and TikTok and so on.” Just a few weeks ago at the Venice Film Festival, the Gaza humanitarian crisis became a huge talking point at the festival with NAZA , a documentary about the killing of Palestinian civilians by Israeli forces in Gaza, taking a special jury prize at the festival. That film was directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and just this week , Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to “revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world.” As a progressive festival, San Sebastián has refused to shy away from the conversation: Last year, the festival issued an open letter calling for an “immediate ceasefire” in Gaza, a unique move for any film festival. It publicly stated its “rejection of the genocide [and] of the unimaginable massacres to which the government of Benjamin Netanyahu is subjecting the Palestinian people since Hamas perpetrated the terrorist attack of 7 October 2023, which, we of course, also condemn.” This year, Rebordinos says its stance remains the same and stresses that festivals and individuals who have a platform should be inclined to use it for speaking about human rights. “I think when you have a possibility to speak to the world, you have to speak about human rights,” he says. “It’s not about taking a position on the left or the right. I have always said that in San Sebastián, all people are welcome. The people who are not welcome are fascists, the people who are against freedom. That is not welcome in San Sebastián. When you are watching Israel kill people – civilian people – I think you have to say something. We can be a small but loudspeaker to the world. “I don’t have anything against the Israeli people – nothing. In fact, this year’s New Directors section has an Israeli member of the jury – Dana Blankstein Cohen. But at the same time, we can’t deny that in this moment, the government of Israel and the military of Israel are killers.” The 74th San Sebastian Film Festival takes place September 18-26, 2026. title: Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed  From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘Naza’ Firestorm
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘Naza’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race Oscars: Italy Unveils 21-Title Shortlist With Nanni Moretti’s ‘It Will Happen Tonight’ & Venice Orizzonti Prizewinner ‘The House Of The Monkey’ View All September 17, 2026 5:50am Naza co-directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at the Venice Film Festival Aurore Marechal/Getty Images The Israeli Film Council has called for film festivals to be eliminated from a points system used to set film fund budgets in the wake of the Venice Film Festival’s selection of bombshell documentary Naza exposing Israel ’s deliberate targeting of civilian targets in Gaza. At the same time, it has also recommended a new state backed funding strand for films celebrating the “heroism” of Israeli soldiers. The body, which advises the Israeli Ministry of Culture film policy, made the recommendations following an emergency meeting called in the wake of the Naza world premiere in Venice last week where it garnered a 25-minute ovation and won the Special Jury Prize. Related Stories News Ireland Boycotts Eurovision Again Over "Appalling Loss Of Lives In Gaza" News Netanyahu Moves To Get 'NAZA' Directors' Israeli Citizenship Revoked The incendiary documentary, revolving around the testimony of 24 Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers which have since been challenged by the Israeli army, has prompted a political firestorm in Israel. Watch on Deadline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to strip Israeli co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of their citizenship, while prominent filmmakers Ari Folman, Shlomi Elkabetz, Ran Tal and Michal Aviad have signed a petition expressing their solidarity for the pair. In a note forwarded to Deadline by an Israeli producer, the Israeli Film Council explained the motivations for its recommendations. “The move is meant to counter the smear and defamation campaigns being waged against Israel worldwide, while also strengthening films that reflect Israeli life and the memory of fallen soldiers’ heroism,” it wrote. It said the recommended new funding strand would support films “centered on the heroism of IDF soldiers and veterans of Israel’s wars who fought to secure the state’s existence, in keeping with the spirit of Israel’s Memorial Day Law for Fallen Soldiers.” The removal of film festivals as one of the criteria deciding film fund budgets will likely further isolate the Israeli cinema industry. The industry’s international standing has plummeted in the wake of Israel’s military operation in Gaza, which was in turn triggered by Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. It is a shadow of its former self, battered by boycotts on one side, and pressure from Netanyahu’s nationalist, rightwing government on the other. Under Israel’s complex state film funding system, the budget for cinema, which currently comes in at around 130m Israeli Shekels ($42m), is divided between six funds. They comprise the country’s oldest film fund, Israel Film Fund, which has recently supported films such as Sundance-selected Oscar entry Tell Me Everything ; Berlinale 2026 title Where To? by Assaf Machnes and Nadav Lapid’s Yes !, a satire critiquing Israeli society in the wake of October 7 and the Gaza military campaign, which was considered to hot to handle for Cannes’s Official Selection and played in Directors’ Fortnight instead in 2025. They are joined by more recently created entitles The New Fund for Cinema & Television; The Makor Foundation for Israeli Film and Television; The Jerusalem Film & Television Fund, and The Yehoshua Rabinovich Foundation for the Arts and the Gesher Multicultural Film Fund. The funds put in tenders for state finance, with their eventual award decided on a points system assessing their recent performance in which the number of A-list festival selections for the films they have backed has traditionally been one of the criteria. “The funds are competing between themselves for the funds from the Israeli Film Council, and one of the things contributing to their final grade is if they have A-list festival films,” explained the Israeli producer. “It was an important criterion but it’s not about the films but rather the motivations of the funds. When funds decide to support a film, one of the things that they consider is whether a director is known or not, say like Ari Folman. The likelihood of his films going to an A-list festival is one of the things that might convince the fund to invest. It’s not the only thing, of course, but it is an important factor along elements like the screenplay, budget,” they said. The producer continued that the Israeli Film Council statement was on one level “empty rhetoric” because Naza was not financed with any Israeli state money, or support from local broadcasters. It was produced instead by Guardian Documentaries with JW Films in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. “ Naza was not funded by Israeli funds or Israeli television, for sure,” they said. “They didn’t approach them, they didn’t apply. “That’s why these recommendations are so funny. Firstly, they want to take away the film festival marks… and then they want to glamorize the IDF. This is really like North Korea. It’s more funny than sad… it idiotic.” In the backdrop, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on Wednesday that he is fast-tracking two bills through parliament in response to Naza , the first revoking the citizenship of anyone who “defames Israeli soldiers”, and the second ratcheting up potential damages payments in successful defamation cases against bodies or individuals maligning the Israeli military. Netanyahu’s threat to revoke Abraham and Szor’s citizenship follows in the wake of a similar threat by Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar, even though he has no legal power to set in motion such a move. If Abraham and Szor, who are both Jewish and born in Israel, were to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship it would unprecedented. While Palestinians with Israeli citizenship have been stripped of citizenship and deported to the West Bank or Gaza, no Jewish Israeli citizen has ever had their citizenship revoked. In the late 1990s, there were calls for the citizenship of Yigal Amir, who assassinated former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995, to be removed. The Supreme Court refused the request. Alongside the political threats, Abraham and Szor have received multiple death threats, with far-right Israeli activists gathering outside the home of the latter’s parents chantings slogans such “death penalty for traitors”. The Brussels-based Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has condemned the attacks and suggested the government rhetoric is putting the filmmakers’ live in danger. “Israeli authorities must ensure the safety of Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and immediately reject any attempt to use citizenship rights as a weapon against journalists,” it said in a statement this week. “Threats from senior government officials can have a chilling effect on journalists and encourage members of the public to engage in intimidation and silencing against them. These threats cannot be dismissed as political rhetoric. They are a warning to journalists and sources about the potential consequences of reporting critically on powerful institutions—and a dangerous signal to other journalists considering whether to investigate or expose alleged wrongdoing.” Netanyahu Moves To Revoke ‘NAZA’ Directors’ Citizenship Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix, Report Finds Australia’s Stan Reviving Rural Drama ‘McLeod’s Daughters’ California Exit Plan Takes Shape Amid Antitrust Battle Over $111B WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

title: Ireland Boycotts Eurovision Again Over “Appalling Loss Of Lives In Gaza”
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Channel 4 Rules Out Reviewing Record Executive Pay Amid Dramatic Job Cuts Wonder Studios: AI Producer Expands LA Office By Hiring CAA Agent & Ex-Westbrook Executive ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ Trailer Offers First Glimpse Of Players Including Bella Ramsey & Maya Jama: “We’re In Game Mode Now” View All September 17, 2026 5:30am Eurovision Song Contest 2026 Sarah Louise Benentt/EBU Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year in a row amid Israel ‘s expected involvement in the 2027 event. In a statement, Irish broadcaster RTÉ said: “RTÉ is today confirming that its position regarding participation in the Eurovision Song Contest remains unchanged. RTÉ will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, nor will RTÉ broadcast the competition. “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk. RTÉ also remains deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory.” Related Stories News Netanyahu Moves To Get 'NAZA' Directors' Israeli Citizenship Revoked News 'We Will Dance Again' Exec Joins Israel's Yoav Gross Productions To Run Content Ireland becomes the second nation to pull out of the Eurovision Song Contest after Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS said it would not participate in 2027. Watch on Deadline Martin Green, director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said: “We regret that RTÉ will not be participating in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027, but we fully respect their decision and recognise the huge contribution they have made to the Contest. They remain a valued part of our family and will be missed. “The Eurovision Song Contest is at its best when broadcasters and their artists from different countries come together to share music, celebrate creativity and create connections between audiences. That power to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the Contest so special, and is even more important now in an increasingly difficult and divided world. “All broadcasters decide on an annual basis to participate in the following year’s Contest. We will remain in dialogue with RTÉ and hope to welcome them back to the Contest in the future.” In December 2025, European broadcasters voted indirectly to allow Israel’s Kan to participate. Green has said that European Broadcasting Union members had spoken “conclusively” and there would not be another vote. Israel finished second in the 2026 contest, which was won by Bulgaria . The 2027 event will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the final hosted at the Arena Burgas on May 15. title: BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe’s Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 5:30am PT BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe’s Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum The four major players respectively were saluted as broadcaster, investor/distributor and producer of the year, with Gao Shan bringing home the very first Ecoprod Cartoon Tributes for its commitment to sustainability in animation. By Kevin Giraud Plus Icon Kevin Giraud Latest BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe’s Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum 2 hours ago Upcoming Canadian Animated Series Shine At Cartoon Forum 2026 1 day ago Heartfelt, Rare Animated Belgian Feature ‘Juul’ Headlines Studio 100 Film’s Expanding Slate at TIFF Market 3 days ago See All 'The Broos,' Courtesy of Bobby Prod Cartoon Forum , the leading co-production event in Europe for animated series, has unveiled the winners of this year’s Cartoon Tributes, recognizing the dedication and creativity of key players in the European animation industry. Chosen by the event’s attendees gathered in Toulouse, the winners in the three established categories (Producer, Broadcaster and Investor/Distributor of the Year) were celebrated today as the Forum slowly comes to a close after three days of intense pitching sessions, networking and debates around the state of European animated TV industry. Related Stories 'Like ‘Amores Perros,’ I Hope My Film Will Also Transcend Time in Some Way,’ Says Gael García Bernal of His Third Directorial Outing, ‘Hombre al Agua’ Water Crisis Documentary 'Every Living Thing' Sets Toronto Market Debut, Adds VIBE as Strategic Partner (EXCLUSIVE) This year, the Producer of the Year went to Bobby Prod (France), who presented “The Broos” back in 2024 at Cartoon Forum. Now streaming on ARTE France, the series (which originated on social media before being developed as an animated series in co-production with ARTE) highlights the potential of digital-first storytelling to reach wider audiences, with creators and communities deeply tied together. Popular on Variety An approach that’s been at the heart of Bobby Prod for more than 15 years, as the studio built its strong identity around irreverent humour, creative freedom and bold storytelling. From bringing known IPs to life with “Creatures Commandos” or “Dead Cells,” Bobby Prod and sister company Bobbypills are now expanding into their own originals IPs with French hit queer animated feature “ Jim Queen ” now being presented at TIFF, and Jordan Firstman announced as lead voice cast. France’s Folivari International takes home the Investor/Distributor of the Year award. Two year since its creation by Folivari, the independent sales agency carefully built its distinctive slate blending in-house titles and third-party acquisitions, with hit series such as “Samuel,” and buzzy titles currently in production and/or development, such as “Pil’s Adventures,” “Ted & Paula’s Tadpole Journey,” “Nino Dino” and “The Baker Street Four,” all presented at Cartoon Forum. BBC , UK’s public-service broadcaster and a major player in the global economy of animated TV series, received the Broadcaster of the Year award, emphasizing the enduring ties between European animation and the post-Brexit United Kingdom. With its children’s services CBeebies and CBBC catering respectively to preschool and school-age audiences, BBC remains a major commissioner and co-producer of children’s animation, with a strong focus on original content and partnerships with independent production companies. A long-standing presence at Cartoon Forum, BBC boarded several European series to its slate after their Forum pitches, including “Duck & Frog,” “Maddie + Triggs,” “Piggy Builders,” “Pablo” and “Dungeons & Kittens.” This year’s Tributes also introduced a fourth category, the Ecoprod-Cartoon Tribute, honoring a European animation production company or initiative that has made a significant contribution to advancing sustainability in the sector. Presented in partnership with Ecoprod, a French non-profit organisation supporting the audiovisual industry’s environmental transition, the new award featured three nominees, with the winner selected by Ecoprod in recognition of its commitment to sustainability across its operations, production methods and storytelling. The very first Ecoprod-Cartoon Forum Tribute went to French, Réunion Island-based Gao Shan Pictures , a 2D and 3D animation service studio and production company creating bold, distinctive and meaningful films for international audiences with sustainability at its core. A stance that is reflected both in the stories it chooses and in the way they are produced, with credits including “ In Waves ,” “The Smurfs,” “Jim Queen” and “Allah is Not Obliged.” At Cartoon Forum 2026, Gao Shan Pictures presented “The Roots of My Hair,” a 2D animated series for teenagers aged 12 to 15 adapted from the eponymous best-selling graphic novel. This year, all nominees had strong ties to Cartoon Forum, having participated in the event both to pitch their projects and to connect with the European animation industry. Companies from the Czech Republic, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Spain and Sweden were also among this year’s nominees. Created in 1990 to boost the co-production and distribution of European animation across television and new media platforms, Cartoon Forum has since helped more than a 1,000 1,053 animation series obtain financing, totaling more than €3.83 billion ($4.39B). It is the first time that bundles have been made available via Premium Subscriptions, which is essentially Roku’s version of a channel store.
