title: Dolly Parton Posthumously Accepts Americana Award in Newly Released Video Recorded Before Her Death: ‘Just Know That I Will Always Love You’
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 5:10am PT Dolly Parton Posthumously Accepts Americana Award in Newly Released Video Recorded Before Her Death: ‘Just Know That I Will Always Love You’ By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Dolly Parton Posthumously Accepts Americana Award in Newly Released Video Recorded Before Her Death: ‘Just Know That I Will Always Love You’ 2 hours ago Tom Petty’s Original Heartbreakers to Reunite for First Time in Decades for Americana Awards, Fronted by Chris Stapleton; Boxed Set of ’70s Rarities Coming 22 hours ago Sheryl Crow Serenaded by Olivia Rodrigo, Chris Stapleton, Jason Isbell and Other Stars at BMI Troubadour Tribute in Nashville 2 days ago See All Courtesy Dolly Parton Estate Some attendees at the Americana Music Honors & Awards might have assumed that the lifetime achievement award for Dolly Parton was something that the Americana Music Association had come up with to honor her in the immediate wake of her death. So a gasp went up from the crowd at the Ryman Auditorium Wednesday night when the lights went down midway through the ceremony and Parton appeared on a big screen to accept the award in what was intended to be in absentia, and would up being posthumous. It wasn’t said when Parton filmed the video, but it was assumed to have been during the summer, which made it all the more startling to see the 80-year-old superstar looking as relaxed, lively and vivacious as she had at any point in recent years. The video acceptance speech was preceded by an introduction from Emmylou Harris , and followed by a tribute performance given by Brandi Carlile and the supergroup trio of I’m With Her (Sarah Jarosz, Aoife O’Donoan and Sara Watkins), singing one of Parton’s most personal signature songs, the autobiographical “Coat of Many Colors.” (Watch video of that performance below.) In the video, Parton says ,”Well, hey, it’s Dolly, and I am so honored to receive the Lifetime Achievement Award from the Americana Music Association. I mean, roots music, or what is now called Americana music, is what I grew up playing back in the Smoky Mountains. It’s that same music that drew me back to East Tennessee back in 1997 to write and record my album ‘Hungry Again.’ “And that project really opened the door to a series of bluegrass and acoustic albums that changed the course of my career in so many ways. Now, new fans discovered these albums, new Americana music communities embraced them, and now, looking back at it all, I see this era of my career as a musical renaissance of sorts.” She concluded, “And I want to thank everybody at the AMA for recognizing me with this award. It’s a great honor, truly. And just know that I will always love you.” Parton receiving the lifetime achievement award was announced just this month, but obviously long in the works. The existence of the acceptance speech was a surprise to the audience, as was the musical performance that followed. On the red carpet, Carlile told Variety , “Dolly’s being honored this year, and that makes me feel really good to be able to be there and bear witness to that.” In her introductory speech, Harris — who collaborated with Parton on the hit “Trio” album, along with Linda Ronstadt — explored her legacy. “Just a few weeks ago, something utterly unthinkable happened: Dolly Parton left our world. But over her time here, this tiny, extraordinary woman made it a better, brighter and kinder place,” Harris said to applause. “One of the many pearls — Dolly would call them rhinestones — of wisdom she imparted was her four-part motto: dream more, learn more, care more, be more,” Harris continued. “Dolly was more from the very start. More than the odds anyone gave her growing up in poverty in Locust Ridge, Tennessee, the fourth of 12 children. More than the precocious 10-year-old who sang on a local TV show. More tha just another pretty woman moving to Nashville with her guitar. And certainly more than the ‘dumb blonde’ she sang about, but never was. “In 1967, Dolly got a good start on her big dream when she landed a gig as the girl singer with Porter Wagoner. All right, remember those? Their duets were a hit on the show and on the charts, but Dolly was nobody’s sidekick. She wanted more and she deserved more, and she set out to get it, always, always, on her own terms. And we all know what happened when Dolly set her sights on something. She didn’t just succeed, she expanded the borders of what a musician could be. “She was a country star, then a pop star, then a global icon. She was one of our all-time greatest songwriters, but she shined just as brightly on stage. She lit up the TV screen and then she lit up the movie screen. Her stunningly beautiful, pure mountain voice could make us cry and then crack us up with a well aimed, sometimes bawdy joke. “There was nothing Dolly couldn’t do, and so she did it. She opened Dollywood, a theme part that continues to provide a real economic boost to the area she grew up in… She created a relief fund that helped hundreds of families get back on her feet after the wildfires ravaged east TN a decade ago. well all remember those. And she saved lives all over the world by funding research that helped lead to a COVID vaccine. Yeah, man, she did that. Closest to her heart was her Imagination Library. it’s given out more than 300 million free books just so far, and that’s showing kids all over the country that they can dream more and be more.” Saying goodbye before the video rolled, “Farewell, Dolly, godspeed, and thank you for everything.” Wednesday’s show had several emotional tributes to the dearly departed. As announced on the morning of the show, six members of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers — original members Mike Campbell, Benmont Tench, Ron Blair and Stan Lynch — reunited in honor of the group’s 50th anniversary, for a lifetime achievement honor. Two additional latter-day members, Steve Ferrone and Scott Thurston, also appeared. The show opened with Chris Stapleton fronting the band for three numbers, “American Girl,” “Breakdown” and “You Wreck Me.” Related Stories Zack Snyder Wants You to Know He’s No Fascist: ‘I Made the Gayest Movie Ever Made’ At the end of the three-and-a-half-hour program, much of the show’s performing cast and winners reemerged on stage for the finale, a tribute to the late Raul Malo of the Mavericks. title: Clare Stewart Steps Down As Rotterdam Managing Director

In her role, Stewart jointly led the organisation alongside Festival Director Vanja Kaludjercic. She will remain in post until next year’s edition, her fourth in the role. Stewart, however, will remain involved with IFFR’s Displacement Film Fund, the short film grant initiative founded and led by Cate Blanchett. IFFR’s Supervisory Board has begun recruiting for a new Managing Director. During Stewart’s tenure, the IFFR team has secured several key funding commitments for the festival and its year-round work. This includes 4-year subsidies from both the National (OCW) and municipal (Gemeente Rotterdam) governments, which see the Festival supported up to and including the 2029 edition, and a successful bid from the content team (led by Chief of Content Melissa van der Schoor) for increased 3-year support from Creative Europe up to and including the 2028 edition. title: Channel 4 Rules Out Reviewing Record Executive Pay Amid Dramatic Job Cuts
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter , Max Goldbart September 17, 2026 4:00am 'The Great British Bake Off' Season 17 Channel 4/Love Productions EXCLUSIVE : Channel 4 has no plans to review record levels of executive pay in recent years despite the UK network’s ambition to radically reduce its cost base. Deadline understands that Channel 4’s board is not giving active consideration to reducing the pay packets of top executives amid a broader strategic review at The Great British Bake Off broadcaster, which will result in 340 layoffs before the end of the year. Alex Mahon and Ian Katz were the highest-paid CEO and chief content officer in Channel 4’s history, and executive remuneration often became a lightning rod for disquiet about the network’s performance. Related Stories News Channel 4 & Paramount's 5 Make History With Advertising Deal News International Insider: European TV In Peril; Venice & TIFF Latest; Mercedes Ron Interview The pay levels contributed to a feeling that Channel 4 became “bloated” and inefficient under Mahon’s regime, with these concerns resurfacing after new CEO Priya Dogra announced last week that the broadcaster will cut more than a quarter of its workforce. Mahon declined to comment. Watch on Deadline Mahon pocketed total pay of £8.46 million ($11.3M) during her tenure, which was up 33% on her predecessor, David Abraham. Katz earned £4.2M in his first six years as chief content officer, a 34% increase on what Jay Hunt was paid during an equivalent period of time. Channel 4 top brass came in for criticism during layoffs in 2024, when it was revealed its top three earners would accept bonuses . Katz ultimately decided to forego his . Channel 4 declined to disclose how much Dogra will be paid, though her earnings will eventually be published next year in the 2026 annual report. Alex Mahon Will Johnston Photography Channel 4’s remuneration committee considers multiple factors when awarding pay, including remit targets, though overall growth is considered a key metric. Channel 4 posted record sales of £1.16 billion on Mahon’s watch in 2021, but the 33% increase in her pay outpaced the company’s revenue growth of 5.6% during her time in charge. Channel 4 chairs have consistently defended executive pay. Interim chair Dawn Airey said last year that Mahon had done an “extraordinary” job in marshalling the company’s resources towards streaming and growing digital ad revenue. Not all agree with Airey. “Executive pay is a tiny proportion of Channel 4’s overall costs, but it’s a perception issue. It speaks to the psychology at Channel 4. The notion that Channel 4 was in rude health under Alex appears to be deception in the context of Priya’s cuts,” said a senior producer, summing up the sentiment of many. “If you want to judge the mess, look at the cleanup.” Swelling Workforce Channel 4 is slashing its workforce by 28%, with around half of commissioning roles at risk. Channel 4’s drama and comedy teams are being smashed together , with talk of seven roles becoming three, encompassing two genre heads under a scripted chief. Film4 is not part of the changes. Insiders said the mood is grim and chaotic. Some criticized the way in which layoffs were handled, including that two different groups were invited to meetings on the same day and “it became quite clear quite quickly which was for redundancy and which wasn’t,” according to one. But Dogra has argued that the changes are essential to ensuring Channel 4 cuts duplication and spends more money on screen. A senior Channel 4 source added that the need to slash costs has been made more urgent by the ad market taking “a dramatic shift down from where all the projections were.” The redundancies have cast light on Channel 4’s workforce swelling in recent years. The company’s average number of employees increased 50% to 1,276 during Mahon’s tenure, a notable period of expansion compared with the BBC, a fellow public service broadcaster, which cut headcount by 20% under former director general Tim Davie. This period included a plan to cut 200 jobs in 2024 , though Channel 4’s average employee numbers only fell by 67 roles during that year. “You always felt like they were bloated and in the end the previous regime’s inaction has meant the current one is now walking off a cliff edge,” said one regular Channel 4 supplier. A former employee lamented: “They’ve known for ages that having about 50 commissioners was wrong, but weren’t brave enough.” Mahon’s allies said she changed internal metrics to include long-term contractors, forcing employee numbers up. Mahon was also responsible for delivering on government demands to grow Channel 4’s presence outside of London, though critics said she chose to do this by duplicating rather than displacing jobs. “To please the politicians, they’ve built these offices and filled them with people, but they haven’t bitten the bullet on how to restructure the center,” said a well-placed industry source. Others pointed out that Channel 4 has made cuts in London and that its Horseferry Road headquarters — which will be put up for sale amid belt-tightening — has been quieter in recent years. A Channel 4 spokesperson said: “It is important to view past remuneration and workforce numbers in the context of one of the most significant periods of transformation in Channel 4’s history. During this time, the organisation managed the impact of the Covid pandemic, expanded its presence across the UK and accelerated its digital transition to a public service streamer. “The organisational changes proposed last week are the first stage of a transformation strategy to prioritise content investment, grow Channel 4’s impact and secure long-term sustainability, and will ensure that the organisation is in the right shape and size to deliver that future.” Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Channel 4/Getty Dogra’s willingness to grasp the nettle of change has impressed insiders and Channel 4 observers, even if there are reservations about her decision to carve up the chief content officer role . Interviews have been ongoing for the director of programmes, with frontrunners said to include BBC iPlayer boss Dan McGolpin and Twofour CEO David Brindley. Numerous key Channel 4 suppliers characterized this hire as being one of the biggest decisions in Channel 4’s 43-year history. “The issues facing Channel 4 go far, and it’s going to take time and real creative leadership to turn things around,” said one. Roughcut CEO Ash Atalla, who produces comedies Big Boys and Stath Lets Flats , is among those who have defended Katz’s record , saying he backed “disruptive shows and the troublemaking that is important to Channel 4.” Dogra has made headway in other ways by poaching Paramount’s £300M TV advertising sales business from Sky, meaning Channel 4 now controls ad sales for Channel 4, 5, and UKTV. David Abraham, Channel 4’s former CEO, said it was the “most significant commercial deal” the company had signed in over a decade. “It brings together a block of the UK airtime and streaming market, which combines UKTV, Channel 4 and Channel 5, to a scale that is material and distinctive enough from what will become the Sky/ITV block,” said Abraham. “It’s a major feather in Priya’s cap and a big achievement to have done it because it’s not easy doing these deals.” Netanyahu Moves To Revoke ‘NAZA’ Directors’ Citizenship Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix, Report Finds Australia’s Stan Reviving Rural Drama ‘McLeod’s Daughters’ California Exit Plan Takes Shape Amid Antitrust Battle Over $111B WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

title: King Charles Makes Rare Statement Over Bombshell Memoir Claim He Told Diana’s Brother: “We’ll Forget Her Soon Enough”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 1:57am King Charles in September 2026 Courtesy of Getty King Charles has, as the British press put it, been dragged into a “war of words” this week with Charles Spencer, the younger brother of the late Princess Diana . Ahead of the release of Earl Spencer’s bombshell memoir about his sibling next week, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister , one particular claim from the book has seemingly thrown the Palace for a loop. Spencer writes that in the wake of Diana’s 1997 death in a Paris car crash, he recalls the then-Prince of Wales saying: “We’ll forget her soon enough.” The uproar among the British public and press has been fierce, and Charles has been criticized for allegedly making such a cruel comment about his ex-wife, who remains a beloved icon in the U.K. — no matter how unpopular other royals are. Related Stories Movies Zhang Yimou to Lead Busan Film Festival Competition Jury Movies Why Aura Entertainment Isn't Obsessed With Topping 'Obsession' Such is the backlash that the Palace has made a rare public statement over the matter, where the firm appears to cast doubt on Spencer’s recollection of the event: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” it said, per BBC News . The language, reporters have pointed out, is strikingly similar to Queen Elizabeth’s response to allegations of racism from Prince Harry and Meghan Markle in 2021, when she stated “recollections may vary,” in what was a surprisingly firm response from the monarch. The latest (and very public) quarrel between King Charles and his former brother-in-law has threatened to loom over a big day for the royal family , with Charles, Prince William and Kate Middleton attending events, as well as Prince Harry’s first major appearance since returning to Britain with Markle . Spencer’s book has unearthed a common public sentiment that the royal family is unwilling to show empathy in moments of hardship, especially surrounding the death of Diana. In the released excerpt from the memoir, Spencer claims that Charles unleashed “a stream of anger” over Spencer’s insistence that Diana would not have wanted 15-year-old Prince William and 12-year-old Prince Harry to walk in her funeral procession. Spencer writes: “[Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’.” According to the BBC, the Palace refute the claim. They see it as being “entirely out of character for a man with a deeply compassionate nature, who at the time was dealing with his own grief and that of their two sons.” THR

title: ‘South Park’ Returns as ‘South America’ as Plot Stays Local and Trump-Free
full_text: Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All September 16, 2026 9:50pm South Park on Comedy Central and streaming on Paramount+. Comedy Central Logo text South Park , one of the longest-running comedy series on television, returned to Comedy Central for its 29th season after making the unexpected move of changing the show’s name to “ South America ” — a gag that creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone announced as a possible marketing gimmick but is certainly also a jab at President Donald Trump. Wednesday night’s season premiere provided little explanation as to when and why the name change happened for the fictional Colorado town, but it does offer a vague metaphor for current U.S. politics around immigration. Seasons 27 and 28 of South Park had shifted from the show’s traditional stand-alone episodes to a season-long arc centered on fictionalized happenings within the White House, including President Trump’s clandestine affair with Satan. With the premiere, the show appears to be returning to its traditional format — stand-alone episodes that may still carry overarching themes. It’s not entirely clear whether we’ve seen the last of South Park ‘s satirical Trump character and the supporting cast of cabinet officials, hangers-on and vice-president-turned-lover J.D. Vance, but they’re absent from this one-off episode, which stays within the confines of the titular town. Related Stories TV When and Where to Stream 'South Park' Season 29 (AKA 'South America') TV South Park's 'South America' Rebrand Isn't Going Anywhere in Season 29 Premiere “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of ‘South Park’ to ‘SOUTH AMERICA,'” Parker and Stone said in a Sept. 8 statement announcing the name change. One might have expected the season premiere to show Trump signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” before eventually getting to South Park. Instead, the season begins after the name change has already been accepted — essentially baking the joke into the show, as characters refer to their town as “South America” without question. Only once does a character allude to the name change itself, and it’s clear the moment was divisive for the town. What the episode offers is a straightforward plot that, as usual, hides a metaphor for a social issue beneath dialogue soaked in double entendres. It begins with Eric Cartman faking being bullied at school to trick his mother into buying him an e-bike — a vehicle clearly designed for adults that has become the one thing every kid in town must have. Ever the earnest pushover, Liane Cartman complies, and soon the boy is terrorizing the town on his new, dangerous ride. Eventually, more of the town’s children are wreaking havoc around South America, crashing through diner windows and scaring pedestrians — a clear metaphor for groups of immigrants moving into American towns. Early in the episode, Kyle tries his own version of Cartman’s ploy on his mother, but he has to go through his father, Randy, who arrives home in flashy spandex and sneakers, now a 10-speed cyclist commuting in the bike lane that’s being overtaken by kids on e-bikes. Randy soon forms a gang of 10-speed riders that begins roughing up anyone in their way. They’re not especially fast, though — one motorist bemoans the “old farts” blocking the road. Still, the gang feels like a stand-in for Immigration and Customs Enforcement as they comb the town trying to eradicate the e-bike kids. As the kids’ South American youth biker gang is hunted by Randy’s gang of adults, the episode piles on satire aimed at the companies and public figures who have fallen in line as Trump took a marker to traditional maps. Google is repeatedly used to search things like “how to get the laws changed in South America?” (the answer: bribing government officials) and “how can police respond to gang violence in South America?” (the answer: extreme violence). The episode also spoofs the massive cultural anticipation ahead of the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , the video game sequel slated to arrive in stores in November — making it a natural stand-in for the upcoming midterm elections, which “the libs” of Trump’s America are looking to for drastic change. “Hopefully, things will get better in November. That’s when Grand Theft Auto Six comes out,” one character says. Someone has to do something — we need to get these kids off the streets and back inside on their phones. Parker and Stone have packed these metaphors into the premiere, a style that marks a clear departure from last season’s grotesque White House storylines. The question now is whether they plan to run this metaphor across the season and carry on with the e-bikes plot or if they will bring a new issue into the foreground and subject it to their now more subtle satire. title: Bleachers Bring Out The Chicks to End Five Nights of Underplays at the Troubadour
full_text: × Skip to main content By Rachel Head Plus Icon Rachel Head View All September 16, 2026 8:11pm Bleachers performed their fifth and final show at the Troubadour on Tuesday, Sept. 15. Rachel Head Bleachers ended a rare set of underplays in Los Angeles at West Hollywood’s Troubadour on Tuesday night, bringing out The Chicks to close out a full-circle moment marking the first time the New Jersey indie rockers have played the iconic venue since 2014. Led by Grammy-winning superproducer Jack Antonoff, Bleachers gave fans a much closer look than usual in the 500-cap room, with their nostalgic sound and deep-cut lyrics right at home with the Troubadour’s magic. The Troubadour gave a much more intimate vibe than the arenas and theaters they usually play, like Madison Square Garden back in June. With the smaller space, the band could engage directly with the audience more freely, with devotees in the front row feet away at the edge of the stage. Related Stories Music Ed Sheeran Openers Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe Depart Tour in Solidarity With Macklemore TV Noah Kahan Performs "Bridge Over Troubled Water" During 2026 Emmy In Memoriam All five nights felt like a return to the start of the group, with the set list offering a blend of nostalgia from their first album, Strange Desire , and fresh cuts from everyone for ten minutes , the band’s fifth studio album they released in May. Showcasing old favorites and new material, concertgoers were given a compilation of cherished classics like “Don’t Take the Money” and “Good Morning” and new songs including “you and forever” and the everyone for ten minutes’ opening song “sideways,” which kicked off Tuesday’s show too. The inclusion of an acoustic set further heightened the intimacy, with Antonoff’s vocals shining. Past the midway point of their set, they’d brought up country icons The Chicks for a surprise guest appearance for a cover of “I Wanna Get Better,” which sent the audience into a frenzy. Carly Rae Jepsen performed the same song — originally released by Bleachers in 2014 on their debut album — with Antonoff on the first night. Tuesday’s show also featured Antonoff’s dad, Ricky Antonoff, who joined the band for “How Dare You Want More.” Despite the venue’s capacity of just 500, concertgoers radiated an electric energy, creating a vibrant and lively atmosphere. Some in the crowd brought bubbles to spray during a few songs, adding a funny extra dynamic during some of the slower, more emotional songs like “Merry Christmas, Please Don’t Call,” the band’s melancholy tune about setting emotional boundaries and asking a toxic person not to contact you during the holidays. Bleachers’ mini-residency served as a good reminder of the importance of connecting popular bands with intimate venues, championing not just the music but also the shared joy between the band and their fans. For some, this was their first Bleachers show, and others their 19th, 30th or, in one fan’s case, their 98th. Bleachers may have graduated from their time in these smaller rooms, but this past week’s stand at the Troubadour is a reminder that it’s still magical when artists make their way back to those intimate spaces they began their careers in. title: Universal Is Getting Cold Feet on Releasing the Elon Musk Documentary (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All September 16, 2026 7:44pm Elon Musk, founder and CEO of SpaceX, speaks via video before the ringing of opening bell at the Nasdaq Marketsite at the launch of the company's initial public offering (IPO) on June 12, 2026 in New York City. Musk is the subject of a hard-hitting documentary that Universal may back out of releasing. Spencer Platt/Getty Images When it screened at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, Musk got the kind of reception every international distributor dreams about. Attendees applauded enthusiastically for five minutes and saluted director Alex Gibney , even shouting “thank you” inside the festival’s Sala Grande for his hard-hitting investigation into the world’s richest man. But despite that instant and reassuring focus group, Universal Pictures , which controls worldwide rights to the film outside of North America, now appears to be having second thoughts on a documentary it paid a significant sum to acquire. The company has not dated the movie, has not communicated with the filmmaking team about its plans, and generally appears to be rethinking the release of a project that it once showed high enthusiasm for but is now politically sensitive for parts of the Trump administration. Two people with knowledge of the dynamic who were not authorized to speak publicly tell The Hollywood Reporter that while a final decision has not been made and that several outcomes were possible, they believed that Universal would ultimately decide against releasing the film and return rights to the movie to filmmakers. When asked what its release plans were for the film, a Universal representative said it had no comment. The movie is set to premiere in U.S. theaters via the independent Bleecker Street as well as play the London Film Festival next month; both are media-rich affairs that a studio usually times with a release in the U.K. and even across the European continent. But Universal has made no such plans. Gibney did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment. If Universal opts against releasing the movie, it would mark an extraordinary reversal at a moment when media companies are already under scrutiny for bowing to various forms of political pressure. Amazon backed out of releasing Artificial as it got into business with Sam Altman’s OpenAI, while ABC News and Paramount/CBS News each paid millions to settle lawsuits with the Trump administration many legal experts felt would be quickly dismissed. Universal would be required to pay filmmakers a kill fee not to release the movie, according to a person familiar with the deal’s structure. The filmmakers would then be free to sell it anew, essentially allowing it to profit twice off the same rights sale. The film would not struggle to be seen around the world no matter what happens. Distributors in individual countries have been salivating over the film ever since the four-hour project began gaining buzz in recent weeks, first with a THR cover story and then with the Venice and Toronto festival premieres, but were of course told it was spoken for, and many would likely jump at a fresh chance to buy it. Still, the specter of yet another media giant paying a bounty to avoid angering people on the right while also shelving a project for no legitimate creative reason would surely raise questions about the ability of conglomerates to protect free speech in an era when it is already under assault. Musk is a politically explosive film that alleges, among other things, that its subject could be using data gathered during his DOGE period against Democrats in the upcoming U.S. election. In the film Gibney includes comments from Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning godfather of AI, describing how that could play out. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” he says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on U.S. citizens. And what DOGE did looked like just what you would do.” While Donald Trump’s relationship with Musk has had his ups and downs, Musk has had a rock-solid relationship with FCC chair Brendan Carr, who had come to Musk’s defense when the Biden administration opened investigations into the mogul, has allegedly facilitated Starlink regulatory approvals and even posed for a praise-filled selfie with him. An FCC source who has worked closely with Carr said he privately reveres the tycoon. And Carr, of course, oversees an agency that wields enormous power over media companies and currently is conducting an investigation into Comcast’s DEI practices. Angering Carr with a Musk release could potentially bring more legal and regulatory headaches for the Brian Roberts-led conglomerate. Universal bought the rights to Musk three years ago, paying a multimillion dollar price tag to release the film around the world. But the climate was very different in 2023, with Musk not yet aligning formally with Donald Trump and the 45th president — and Carr — far from the apex of power. Musk has shown his disdain for Gibney’s film, repeatedly calling it a “hit piece” and saying it was “boring,” despite the fact that there are no indications he has seen it. His lawyer, Alex Spiro, has also sent a letter to Gibney’s production company putting it “on notice,” raising the temperature for potential distributors. HBO snapped up North American TV and streaming rights back in 2023 and pressed Gibney to continue shooting when Musk arrived in Washington at the start of the Trump administration, even dipping into its coffers to provide more financing. For now the company is plowing ahead, though a sale of Warner Bros Discovery to David Ellison could complicate the picture. Ellison’s father Larry, who is partly bankrolling the WBD acquisition, is briefly cited in the film in an unfavorable light. The earliest HBO could air the film is February given a four-month pay VOD window retained by the filmmakers. By February, Ellison could already control HBO and WBD. THR

title: Matthew Lillard Says He’s “Embarrassed” About Returning for ‘Scream 7’ After Melissa Barrera’s Firing
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All September 16, 2026 7:24pm Matthew Lillard and Melissa Barrera Jesse Grant/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures; Arturo Holmes/Getty Images Matthew Lillard has confessed that he’s “embarrassed” about returning for Scream 7 following Melissa Barrera’s firing from the slasher franchise. During a recent Q&A, via a video posted on TikTok , the actor said Barrera was “on the right side of history” when she expressed support for Palestinians in 2023 amid the Israel-Hamas war. “It’s just human, it’s like who we are… I don’t know what else to do,” Lillard said. “For me… I have queer kids; if I’m not standing up for queer kids or kids in the trans community, what the fuck am I doing?” Related Stories Movies Watermelon Pictures Acquires 'Thirteen in Gaza' Out of TIFF (Exclusive) Music Ed Sheeran on Dropping Macklemore From Tour Over Palestine Remarks: "The Promoter's Decision, Not Mine" The Five Nights at Freddy’s star continued, “Listen, I don’t think it’s easy all the time. Melissa Barrera , who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said. … That’s really fucking bullshit and really hard, and she’s on the right side of history. And when they start coming after your job, sometimes things are worth it.” “But I’m just gonna say, what happened to Melissa, the whole world didn’t pipe up,” he added. “She was like a year early on what the fuck’s going on, but the whole world should have piped up and said, ‘She’s right,’ and they didn’t. And that’s brutal.” Lillard said he then “got called out” for reprising his role as Stu Macher in Scream 7 , which was released in February. He previously starred in the original 1996 Scream and 1997’s Scream 2 . “I’m like, ‘Oh fuck, that’s brutal.’ I feel bad about that, I feel shame about that,” he said. “Because in that moment, I was so excited to go back, I didn’t really think about Melissa and the journey, and I didn’t say ‘no.’ And I’m embarrassed, and that’s the truth.” Barrera was dropped from the seventh installment in the slasher franchise in November 2023 after she spoke out in support of Palestine on her social media after Hamas invaded Israel the month prior. Spyglass Media Group, the company behind the Scream franchise, said in a statement at the time, “Spyglass’ stance is unequivocally clear: We have zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech.” Following the news, Jenna Ortega dropped out of Scream 7 , as did director Christopher Landon . Neve Campbell was later brought back to reprise her role as Sidney Campbell in the new film. THR
